Apple has officially entered a new era, with John Ternus taking over as CEO on September 1 after Tim Cook completed 15 years at the top of the company.

Apple first announced the leadership transition in April, confirming that its board unanimously approved Ternus as Cook’s successor. Cook has moved into the role of executive chairman, where he will remain involved with Apple and assist with areas including the company’s relationships with policymakers around the world.

John Ternus begins his new role as Apple CEO

Ternus joined Apple in 2001 and spent years working across the company’s hardware organization. He eventually became senior vice president of Hardware Engineering, overseeing teams responsible for products including the iPhone, iPad, Mac and AirPods. articles.title: Diagnosing sentiment in my typo-reporting workflow
articles.subtitle: This is more of a comment than a question. A few months ago I added a “Report a Typo” feature to Six Colors. The goal was to give people a simple place to go — sixcolors.com/typo …
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
A few months ago I added a “Report a Typo” feature to Six Colors. The goal was to give people a simple place to go — sixcolors.com/typo — if they found a mistake on the website. That Google form inserts the information into a Google Sheet, and a script attached to the Google Sheet kicks off a simple automation that sends me a notification in a couple different places.

This works pretty well. I’m using a very simple Google Apps script to fire off a webhook when there’s a new form submission. The webhook is running on Make.com, which we use for a bunch of simple web automations, but that’s an implementation detail. Make.com posts an item in a private Discord channel and also crafts a custom push notification to my phone using Pushover.

However, the moment I turned this feature on, I discovered the problem with asking people to report errors or typos: Some people see any open channel of communication as an open channel for any sort of communication. I immediately started getting more “this is more a comment than a question” items about articles than actual typo submissions. Commentary included personal preferences for writing style, web design, political references (real or imagined), and much more.

I’m going to make an admission: This sort of feedback is maddening. I want to be alerted promptly about mistakes on the site so I can fix them promptly, but I am not interested in receiving push notifications regarding your opinion of the professionalism and appropriateness of my writing style.

Unfortunately, it’s an open form. There’s nothing to be done. Or is there?

This is a challenge that can’t really be solved by looking for a bunch of keywords. You need wholesale sentiment analysis of the entire submission. This is—brace yourself—actually a good use of a large language model.

I solved this problem by using a plug-in within Make.com that lets me get a reply back from a cloud LLM that uses a simple model with an API cost of pennies per use, but you could also just use Shortcuts to build a version of this automation that runs on a Mac (Tahoe or Golden Gate) using Apple’s built-in models. It works just fine in Shortcuts on my Mac, via the Use Model action. (See screenshot above.)

Here’s the prompt I’m currently using:

Your task is binary classification. Input: a user-submitted comment about an article, claiming to report an error. Output: one token only: ALLOW or REJECT. Definition of ALLOW: A concrete, objective, verifiable issue in the article.

This includes: * factual mistakes * spelling, grammar, formatting mistakes * broken or incorrect links * wrong names, dates, numbers * technical inaccuracies * omissions of material consequences of a feature or change (e. g. , failing to mention that a feature deletes stored Wi-Fi passwords) Definition of REJECT: Anything subjective.

This includes: * political disagreement * tone or style complaints * metaphor or comparison preferences * ‘you should have covered X more’ * speculation about motives * emotional reactions or rants * admissions that it’s not actually a mistake Classification rules: 1. If the comment identifies a specific factual, technical, or materially consequential issue in the article, return ACCEPT. 2.

If the issue would meaningfully affect reader understanding or use of a product/feature, treat it as an omission and return ACCEPT. 3. If the comment is opinion, taste, politics, vibe, personal criticism, or preference, return REJECT. 4. If there is no concrete, verifiable claim about the article being wrong or incomplete, return REJECT. 5. If it’s off-topic or spam, return REJECT. 6.

If it’s a short but simple phrase like “there not their” or “r/sheild/shield”, those are nerdier folks reporting typos and that’s fine, ACCEPT. Respond with exactly one of these two tokens: ALLOW or REJECT. No explanation. Submission: [[insert report text here]]

articles.title: Meta launches Muse Voice Transcribe for real-time voice dictation on Mac
articles.subtitle: Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.

Muse Voice Transcribe powers system-wide dictation on Mac

Meta Superintelligence Labs says Muse Voice Transcribe combines streaming automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization and endpointing.

In practical terms, it can transcribe speech as it happens, separate speakers across recordings with 20-plus voices, and determine when someone has finished talking, all without a separate post-processing step.

The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 validated at launch. It supports audio longer than an hour, plus native code-switching within or between sentences. Language, keyword, and context biasing can further improve recognition.

Rather than using one fixed tradeoff between speed and accuracy, Muse Voice Transcribe decides how long to listen before committing each word. Meta calls this “adaptive delay.” The system can move quickly through easier speech while using more audio context for difficult words.

Meta says the model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis streaming speech-to-text leaderboard as of September 1.

Muse Voice Transcribe is available today through the Meta Model API for $3 per 1,000 audio-minutes, equivalent to $0.18 per hour.

It is also already powering dictation in Meta AI for Mac and Muse Code. On Mac, users can hold the Fn key to dictate into any application.

Apple Intelligence

Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.

Reuters reports that three sources described the China-specific model as a departure from Apple’s strategy of relying on third-party models.

Alibaba reportedly supported the model’s training, though neither company commented.

Models including ChatGPT and Claude are unavailable in mainland China, making Apple’s strategy there different from its approach in other major markets for now.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Previous reporting said Alibaba’s Qwen model and technology from Baidu would be incorporated into the localized system.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

Elsewhere, Apple’s overhauled Siri AI is scheduled to launch publicly with iOS 27 this fall where available.

It will initially support select English variants, while iPhone and iPad availability in the EU is delayed. China’s timeline remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: No Rest for the Wicked, which was slated to hit 1.0 a month before Grand Theft Auto 6, is delayed into 2027
articles.subtitle: Moon Studios said the extra time will "help us improve performance, tighten the class system, and polish the whole game," and made no mention at all of GTA 6.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Moon Studios announced today that its upcoming action RPG No Rest for the Wicked will not go into 1.0 release in October as planned, but will instead launch in March 2027, following an open beta test currently slated for December.

"The honest truth is that we're a small team, and we're holding our games to a standard we won't compromise on," the studio wrote in a Steam update. "We're close, but close isn't good enough for our full 1. 0 launch. The extra time will help us improve performance, tighten the class system, and polish the whole game to the standard you all deserve.

We'd rather take a few more months than ship something that we know isn’t quite perfect yet. "This extra time also means more closed and open beta tests in the coming months, which means you, our community, can get your hands on it and help us shape the final 1. 0 build. " That will include the open beta in December, details of which will be shared in the future.

I should note here that absolutely no mention was made of Grand Theft Auto 6, which comes to consoles in November, in either the Steam update or a video message posted by Moon Studios chief Thomas Mahler.

Some studios have made a point of avoiding the GTA 6 behemoth, others are theatrically charging straight at it; it's impossible to say how much of a role Rockstar's monster played in the decision to push No Rest for the Wicked into 2027, if any, but at the very least I imagine it has to be considered a nice side effect.

Regardless, this really isn't the most devastating delay of all time. No Rest for the Wicked launched into early access on Steam more than two years ago, in April 2024, and has since seen significant updates, drawn in nearly 65,000 user reviews, and sold more than a million copies. Moon Studios chief Thomas Mahler warned in January that once 1.0 hits, No Rest for the Wicked's price will be increased from its current $40 to $60.

articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps

Aside from being featured by Apple in the M6 Mac mini launch, Perplexity has been relatively quiet on the Mac front this summer. That changes today with hybrid compute for Mac.

Perplexity first announced work on splitting AI tasks between local and cloud models in June. Today, Hybrid Compute is launching as part of Perplexity’s Mac app.

“Computer now splits a task between cloud models and a local model on your Mac,” the company says.

“Computer starts each task in the cloud. Trigger one from your iPhone, and your Mac accesses your files and runs sensitive steps locally.”

Introducing hybrid compute in Perplexity Computer. Computer can start a task in the cloud, then move to a local model that runs on your Mac. Use it for steps involving private files or sensitive data. Available today in the Perplexity Mac app. pic.twitter.com/bafirGWgwA — Perplexity (@perplexity_ai) September 1, 2026

Perplexity’s website explains how the new feature works:

Our on-device PII classifier reads each task on the Mac before it is sent. Names, addresses, and account numbers are swapped for stand-ins, then restored when the answer returns. We’ve open-sourced the on-device PII classifier, trained in collaboration with Perplexity’s Secure Intelligence Institute.

Macs with 8GB and 16GB RAM won’t be able to run hybrid compute, according to Perplexity. 24GB memory is the minimum, and 32GB is recommended as the floor:

Hybrid Compute runs on Apple silicon, macOS 15+ — 24 GB unified memory minimum, 32 GB for best results. Set up the local model once: download PPLX Qwen 3.8 27B in one click. No Ollama or manual runtime setup. Work it handles uses no cloud credits. No API key.

MacStories also has coverage of the new Perplexity feature today. You can learn more from Perplexity’s announcement page here.

Hybrid compute is just the latest AI tool from Perplexity that takes advantage of the power of the Mac. In May, the company overhauled its Mac app with a whole new version. Apple specifically cites Perplexity Personal Computer as a productivity use case for the new M6 Mac mini as well.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: New 'Street Fighter' Trailer Is About Ken and Ryu’s Beef, but Guile Steals the Show
articles.subtitle: It seems like Ryu and Ken aren't on the best terms The upcoming Street Fighter movie gets more ridiculous and promising with every trailer.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
It seems like Ryu and Ken aren't on the best terms

The upcoming Street Fighter movie gets more ridiculous and promising with every trailer. Paramount Pictures and Legendary just released a new look at the film, highlighting what seems to be its central emotional hook: Ryu and Ken’s strained friendship.

We learn that Ryu (Andrew Koji) hesitantly enters the World Warriors Tournament after Chun-Li (Callina Liang) informs him that his old friend Ken Masters (Noah Centineo) has entered the dangerous competition. Ken resents his training partner and seems dead set on escaping his shadow. There are plenty of homages to the games, like E.

Honda doing his infamous headbutt slam, Ryu whipping out a Tatsumaki spin-kick, and Chun-Li doing Lightning Legs. Ken and Ryu do their fist bump from Street Fighter 3, and David Dastmalchian hams it up as M. Bison; honestly, the film looks like a surprisingly fun time. The best line in the trailer comes when Guile (Cody Rhodes) yells at Dan after suffering a nasty slash to the face.

Legendary also posted a playable version of the trailer where the player/viewer performs quick time event prompts on an arcade cabinet. Many of the inputs are even accurate to the games, such as having the player perform a quarter circle forward motion in time with Ryu launching a Hadouken.

Has there ever been a Street Fighter movie before?

There have been several Street Fighter films in the past. Universal Pictures released the infamous live-action Street Fighter movie starring Jean-Claude Van Damme in 1994. While it was panned at the time, the one bright spot was Raul Julia’s excellent performance as M. Bison.

After Chun-Li recounts the day Bison killed her father, he responds that he doesn’t remember and delivers the iconic line, “For you, the day Bison graced your village was the most important day of your life. But for me, it was Tuesday. ” Beyond the live-action film, Street Fighter II: The Animated Movie was also released in 1994, and it received a more positive reception.

It will be interesting to see whether the upcoming Street Fighter can accomplish the difficult task of bringing the ridiculous world of fighting games to the screen; most previous attempts have fallen flat, with the Mortal Kombat films being the latest example. We’ll find out whether the movie can pull off a reversal when it hits theaters on Oct. 16, 2026.

articles.subtitle: Artificial Intelligence takes center stage in a few of the apps enjoying this week’s spotlight — and not the kind of AI that’s going to have you rolling your eyes or organizing a protest march against the nearest data center.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Artificial Intelligence takes center stage in a few of the apps enjoying this week’s spotlight — and not the kind of AI that’s going to have you rolling your eyes or organizing a protest march against the nearest data center. No, these are actually useful AI features that take some of the busy work of daily life out of your hands so you can concentrate on other things.

AI or no, we’re always looking for top macOS and iOS apps to feature here. If you’ve got something that fits that description, drop us a line at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief outline of the whats, whys, and wherefores.

Now on to this week’s selection…

Sortio

The folders on my Mac are a mess, but who has the time to make sure that everything is filed away in its proper place? AI does, according to the makers of Sortio, a macOS utility that promises to do the hard work of organization on your behalf.

Sortio taps into AI to look at file names and metadata to help it figure out where to put each file. You can also opt to let the utility read the file, sending a 4KB excerpt to your AI provider of choice for even more detailed sorting. (Sortio also offers an offline mode that uses Ollama or LM Studio to keep its activity on your Mac.) You can further refine sorting by telling Sortio to organize things by file type, project, date, and whether the file is for work or personal use..

I took Sortio for a spin, having it go through the folder of articles I’ve written but haven’t bothered to organize for myself. Sortio was smart enough to take my submissions to Awful Announcing and separate them into their own folder. Not every search is that precise — a separate sorting session had Sortio tagging an offer letter from an old employer named Purch as a financial document — but there are edit buttons to correct mislabeled and misfiled material.

You can try out Sortio for free, which gives you enough of an allowance to sort through a few thousand files to get a flavor for how the app performs. After that, you’ll need to buy a license, with the $14.99/month Pro license suitable for most individual users. There are team and enterprise options as well, and paying for an annual license lowers your monthly rate.

AskPlay

AI isn’t just for organizing your folders; it can also generate a playlist for you based on specific artists, songs or moods you’re hoping to hear. At least, that’s the idea behind AskPlay, an app that lives in your menu bar and lets you type or speak plain-English instructions on the type of music you want to listen to.

You’re going to need a few things besides AskPlay and its $1.99/month subscription to make the app work. For starters, AskPlay works exclusively with Apple Music, so you’ll also need to subscribe to Apple’s streaming service. In addition, you’ll need to provide an API key from an AI provider, with AskPlay supporting OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter.

Those requirements are likely to limit AskPlay’s appeal to some users, but having tried out the app on my Mac, I am impressed by the results. I told AskPlay I wanted to hear songs written by Stephen Sondheim, and it dutifully produced a playlist not just from cast soundtracks but also numbers by vocalists from their own albums.

That said, there were a few misfires — the playlist included a song from Tick, Tick… Boom! , a Jonathan Larson musical that only refers to Sondheim, as well as a rap song that shares a title with something Sondheim wrote. Other requests like “play upbeat songs from the ’80s” proved more successful.

An AskPlay feature I appreciate was the ability to augment playlists. After generating a playlist of Merle Haggard songs, I had the app add Johnny Cash music to the queue. Then I told AskPlay to “add more songs like these,” which brought Waylon Jennings, George Jones, and more to the party.

AskPlay seems built for a very specific kind of user, but if you like thematic playlists and already subscribe to the services that make this app tick, it brings another dimension to your listening experience. In addition to working on the Mac, AskPlay is available for a range of Apple devices including the iPhone, iPad and Vision Pro.

Pocket Screen

I don’t know about you, but my workflow often requires me to jump from one window to another to perform a task — and that can often break up my workflow. I’m thinking of when I’m writing something and need to refer to notes I’ve taken in another application or a PDF I have loaded up in Preview. Jumping between apps takes me out of the flow of writing, not to mention that accurately transcribing what’s in one app to the other can occasionally be a hit-or-miss proposition.

Pocket Screen addresses some of that dilemma by creating a floating window of one app that you can keep in view when you’re working on something else. Think of Pocket Screen as a picture-in-picture feature, but for productivity. You can capture a PDF, webpage, video, chat or other kind of information and keep it close at hand in a resizable window that you can move around your desktop. The app supports up to two simultaneous views, according to its developer.

articles.title: Perplexity Introduces ‘Hybrid Compute’ for Computer Agent on Apple Silicon Macs
articles.subtitle: Source: Perplexity. Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based. Recently, Perplexity also introduced Portable Computer, a local-first version of Computer that can escalate work to the cloud with a user’s permission.

Hybrid compute approaches the problem from a different direction. Tasks start in the cloud but if a new local classifier detects potentially sensitive information, the user is alerted and asked whether they want to route it to a local model, although users also have the option to let the flagged data be used by a frontier cloud-based model. Gemma E4B, Qwen3.6 35B-A3B, and a Perplexity post-trained version of Qwen3.6 35B are available at launch for that local work, with more models to come in the future.

Tasks that don’t require sensitive information are handled in the cloud by frontier models that also orchestrate the cloud and local tasks. Users select the cloud orchestrator and Perplexity chooses the helper frontier models used.

Another key feature is that hybrid compute works with tasks begun from an iPhone or iPad, too. Those devices could already kick off a session, but now they can also run tasks that use sensitive information locally if your Mac is turned on and running Perplexity.

Yesterday, I got a demo of the feature that walked through three scenarios:

an attorney researching a legal brief, with sensitive client data on their Mac, allowing them to update it locally,

an analyst using web-based data to update a confidential slide deck for a presentation about a company’s financials, and

a small business owner kicking off pricing research from her iPhone that was combined with private pricing data for her business that never left her Mac.

I haven’t tried hybrid compute myself yet, but if it works as advertised, it’s a big step forward for Perplexity, and one that a lot of its competitors are also chasing. AI agents are only as good as the tools and data to which they have access.

Tool calling has been a big focus over the last year and more, but data privacy is an equally important issue that needs to be solved before more companies, especially those in regulated industries, adopt agentic tools like Personal Computer. It’s good to see Perplexity tackling this head-on.

articles.title: Dwarf Fortress creator says we can learn something from simply walling up dwarf nobles to maintain an equal society—but notes you have to abolish the dwarf cops, too: 'Another lesson to be had there'
articles.subtitle: Much to consider.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
While the legendarily absurd complexity of fantasy simulation in Dwarf Fortress provides countless perils for dwarven health and happiness, the most insidious threat to any mountain hall emerges from within: Nobility. As a fortress flourishes, it inevitably draws the attention of dwarven nobles who'll needlessly burrow themselves into industries they're not qualified to direct, issuing demands and mandates without any care for whether they're feasible or sustainable for the rest of dwarven society.

Sounds unbelievable, I know. But there are ways to manage the menace of nobility—like simply walling them off in an unpleasant corner and letting the rest of society live and labor as need, preference, urgency, and capacity allow. In an interview with PC Gamer at Gamescom, Dwarf Fortress co-creator Tarn Adams said there's probably something to be learned there.

While Dwarf Fortress players are capable of pursuing an egalitarian dwarven utopia, its simulation doesn't yet allow for dwarves to engage with their own political ideologies—but Adams said he's had distant plans to tinker with systems for simulating civilizational law codes, and maybe even some light philosophizing.

"I think there's room for that kind of thing. I read a lot of law codes. I read the Tang law code; Romans had crazy case law, and I read a bunch of commentary about that," Adams said. "And it's funny: I'm not sure about the modern systems, but in the Chinese one from 1500 years ago, it says 'if you know it's wrong, but it doesn't fit any of these 2000 things, you just hit the person 10 times and call it a day.'"

It might sound like a crude solution, but for Adams, it helped conceptualize how a simulated law code could essentially function like a series of conditional statements in computer logic.

"That feels like an if-else-if-else-if-else-if-else-if—and then you have your final else in your law code. I'm like, I can do that. I can model a civil law code," Adams said. "When it comes to case law, it's more like a scripting language that interprets itself. I can also get into that now, especially now that [Dwarf Fortress shifted to Lua scripting.] That's more complicated, but manageable—as long as you've got safety valves to escape from a process completely breaking down."

As for what that process breaking down might look like, Adams said you might have "cases being argued by dwarven barristers or something, but then there'd be a dog wandering into the room and biting somebody. And then the goblins come."

I suspect surviving Roman law commentaries don't offer any immediate guidance there, but in the meantime, Adams reckons that Dwarf Fortress can offer some political wisdom of its own. Being able to literally wall off the vampiric influence of a mountain hall's noble class, he said, is a model that might offer some applicable lessons in our own lives.

"Has been tried, could be tried again. It sounds like a fine thing. Where'd EA go? It's been purchased. So we didn't have a wall there," Adams said. "Could have had a wall. Didn't have a wall. Many such cases. It seems simple to me, but it's complicated somehow."

Adams did note, however—as I have in my own experiments with ushering in dwarven utopia by subjecting the upper classes to a living entombment—that the influence of dwarven nobility persists as long as there's an armed entity enforcing its demands. If your fortress maintains a fortress guard, they'll continue punishing dwarves who violate mandates issued by nobles under wall-arrest.

"If you put a wall around your nobles, their demands still somehow get into the aether, and your little justice system will still punish dwarves," Adams said. "So you have to not assign a captain of the guard either. Another lesson to be had there."

articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
USB-C and its Thunderbolt variant are the most up-to-date standards of the USB connector. They allow data-transfer speeds of up to 80Gbps, can fast-charge devices up to 240W, and conveniently fit in a port either way up—which means that you can wave bye-bye to the age-old USB guessing game of “Which way does it go in?”.

USB-C is no one-trick pony—handling data transfer, video output and power input. You’ll find faster variants of USB-C (called Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5) on Macs. Each version of Thunderbolt is backwards compatible with USB-C so the adapters reviewed here will all work with modern Macs—from the MacBooks Neo, Air and Pro, through to the desktop iMac, Mac mini and Studio.

USB-C’s 5-10Gbps speeds will limit some of Thunderbolt’s more impressive 40 to 80Gbps potential but for most people even 5Gbps is fast enough. If super-fast data transfer is one of your requirements, a number of hubs reviewed below do use Thunderbolt or 40Gbps USB4.

Find out more in our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 comparison and also our chart at the end showing all the ports of Apple’s recent Macs.

Apple

In general, an “ adapter ” works with a single port (such as USB-A or Ethernet) while a “ hub ” gives you multiple ports. If you require even more, then look for a “ docking station ” or “ dock “. Docks usually come with their own power supply, while hubs require a separate USB-C charger if you need a power source. If you’re after a full desktop setup for your MacBook, look out for our recommendations for the best USB-C and Thunderbolt docking stations for MacBooks.

Apple sells its own range of USB-C adapters to HDMI, VGA and more, but they are overpriced and underpowered compared to the premium USB-C hubs and adapters we have reviewed here. We haven’t included the many much cheaper but lower-quality versions you can find online as we recommend only from trusted and tested makers.

Look for each hub’s video capability for connecting to external displays. Most support only one monitor, but some offer two—note that more than two usually requires an extra software install.

Passthrough power will likely also be of interest to MacBook users. 60W Power Delivery (PD) will work even for the 16-inch MacBook Pro (just), but more watts equals a faster charge.

Note that the ports on the MacBook Neo are USB-C and only one of them is properly data-ready at 10Gbps, with the other just for charging. Read more on how the MacBook Neo’s USB-C ports are different. As it has just one data port, a USB-C hub becomes a must for expanding the Neo’s potential—read our roundup of the best MacBook Neo accessories.

Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: Star Trek Is Officially Switching Genre In 2027 With New Release

articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Get ready for a taste of psychological horror through Star Trek's sci-fi lens

Over the past 60 years, Star Trek has maintained its stranglehold on pop culture by boldly exploring a multitude of genres through a sci-fi lens: romance, mystery, courtroom drama, and even the occasional horror story. While the original series and Star Trek: The Next Generation told more traditional and serious sci-fi stories, more recent entries like Lower Decks and Strange New Worlds showed off the sillier side of Trek.

In 2027, Star Trek will make a hard pivot to a new genre familiar to gaming fans: psychological horror. The new Trek release will borrow elements from Alien, Resident Evil, and Dead Space with its approach to sci-fi scares — and it will bring back a fan-favorite Star Trek: The Next Generation character.

Star Trek: Shadow Frontier will officially bring back a TNG icon

Image: Bloober Team/Paramount Games Studio

Silent Hill 2 and Cronos: The New Dawn developer Bloober Team is responsible for Star Trek's next big gamble: Star Trek: Shadow Frontier. Bloober and Paramount Games Studio describe Shadow Frontier as a "new sci-fi psychological thriller title set on a mysterious, uncharted planet."

Star Trek: Shadow Frontier features a face familiar to Star Trek: The Next Generation fans: Ro Laren, the Bajoran officer who often clashed with Starfleet in the late-'80s revival of the Trek franchise. Ro will be played in Shadow Frontier by the actor who originally played her, Michelle Forbes.

According to an official announcement from Paramount Games Studio and Bloober Team, the story of Star Trek: Shadow Frontier takes place on an uncharted planet that Ro crash-lands on after answering a distress call. The unnamed planet is a "spaceship graveyard where nothing is as it seems," the game's creators say, and as she "explores the planet's corrupted surface and crosses paths with other survivors, she must face twisted creatures, a hostile ecosystem, and an entity that seeks to envelop her body and mind."

A teaser trailer for Star Trek: Shadow Frontier offers more questions than answers, but the prospect of Bloober Team exploring sci-fi again after Observer and Cronos: The New Dawn is certainly enticing. Star Trek has dabbled in psychological horror infrequently, so Star Trek: Shadow Frontier will hopefully live up to its exciting premise.

Star Trek: Shadow Frontier is a bold new direction for the franchise

“We’ve long admired the way Bloober Team crafts deeply immersive, atmospheric experiences that keep players on the edge of their seats,” said Shawn Kittelsen, head of creative and production at Paramount Games Studio, in a news release. “For Star Trek: Shadow Frontier, it was essential to partner with a studio that could both honor that legacy and push it forward.

We have full confidence in Bloober’s ability to deliver a game that does justice to the Star Trek name while bringing something bold and new to the beloved franchise. "

“As lifelong fans of science fiction, Star Trek has always held a special place in our hearts,” said Piotr Babieno, CEO of Bloober Team. “By combining that passion with what we do best, horror, we’ve partnered with Paramount to create something truly unique: a new adventure set in a beloved universe, enriched with our own signature layer of dark, psychological thriller.

We’re genuinely excited about this journey, and our hope is to honor the legacy of Star Trek in a way that feels both respectful yet refreshingly different. ”

Bloober Team has a packed slate of games coming. In addition to publishing a new asymmetric multiplayer horror game based on the Saw franchise, the developer is also working on a remake of the original Silent Hill and Layers of Fear 3.

Star Trek: Shadow Frontier is coming to Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X in 2027.

articles.title: The Potential of M6 and M5 Ultra for Local AI on macOS
articles.subtitle: Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio. You can read more details about the announcement and related specs in John’s overview.

As someone who’s been working with an M3 Ultra Mac Studio (on loan from Apple) with 512 GB of RAM for the past year (plus two separate M4 Mac minis) with a particular focus on local AI models and performance gains enabled by Apple’s MLX framework, I obviously am very interested in these new machines.

To give you some context: my current workspace for my upcoming iOS and iPadOS 27 review, which lives in Notion, is entirely managed by a series of local agents running the latest DeepSeek-V4-Flash via MLX on the Mac Studio, which continuously scan the project for new notes, sources, and research material that is automatically categorized and linked in the chapters that I’m writing.

So, yes, I’m sure I’ll have more thoughts on the new Mac minis and Mac Studios soon. In the meantime, I thought it’d be fun to break down the local AI-related details from Apple.

First, the M6. While it may not be the powerhouse that the M5 Ultra is, it’s an interesting new chip because of its new 2 nm process and dual Neural Engine system:

M6 is built using cutting-edge 2 nm process technology, packing greater transistor density into a smaller die for a major leap in performance and power efficiency. M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

But that’s not all: the new 12-core GPU (which has two more cores than the M4’s old GPU) now features Neural Accelerators in each core for the first time on the Mac mini. The result, according to Apple, is “4x faster AI performance and 2x faster graphics than Mac mini with M4”. If these numbers hold up and scale linearly, a local Mixture-of-Experts model such as Qwen 3.

5-35B-A3B, which would run at ~17 tokens/sec on average on a base M4 Mac mini with 16 GB of RAM, could realistically generate output at over 60 tokens/second with the base model M6 Mac mini.

Based on what we’ve seen so far, the one downside of the M6 Mac mini is that it does not have Thunderbolt 5 ports; those are exclusive to the M5 Pro model, also announced today. As Apple also notes, Thunderbolt 5 allows multiple M5 Pro Mac minis to run local AI models as a single cluster (for example, using something like exo ).

Alas, that won’t be possible with the M6 Mac mini and its Thunderbolt 4 bandwidth bottleneck. Nonetheless, I’d be intrigued to compare the performance of the widely regarded Qwen3. 8-27B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash models on the new M6 Mac mini.

Moving on to the flagship M5 Ultra Mac Studio, let’s start here:

With M5 Ultra, Mac Studio achieves up to 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of M3 Ultra and a staggering 9.8x more than M1 Ultra. Combined with up to 512GB of unified memory and 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth, 50 percent higher than before, Mac Studio lets users run massive models entirely on device with complete privacy — without counting tokens or worrying about rising cloud costs.

As seen on the Mac Studio’s product page, the 512 GB RAM version of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio will only be available in “late October”. Unlike the M6, the M5 Ultra supports Thunderbolt 5, which will allow customers to run multiple Mac Studios in a cluster with shared memory to distribute inference across machines. And, according to Apple, a cluster of four Mac Studios yields three times the performance of a single Mac Studio.

Speaking from personal experience, I know that my M3 Ultra Mac Studio using oMLX can run DeepSeek-V4-Flash locally with generation averaging 35 tokens/second. Assuming a linear 4x increase, that would put the same model at over 120 tokens/second on an M5 Ultra Mac Studio.

To put things in perspective, that kind of performance would be faster than any AI chatbot website, it’d be faster than many providers who offer a “fast” mode for their models, and it’d only be second to either dedicated NVIDIA PC clusters at home or specialized inference providers such as Cerebras or Groq …which are running in full-blown data centers.

Sure, you would need a computer that is likely going to cost more than $20,000 to make it happen, but it’d still be possible on a single machine that is small, quiet, and that – in theory – any consumer can buy off the shelf.

It’s also interesting to consider the implications of M5 Ultra for running much larger models that would have typically required aggressive quantization to even stay in memory and produce any useful output. For example, Z. ai’s GLM-5.

2 (a 744B MoE model) could run at up to 17 tokens/second on an M3 Ultra Mac Studio with 512 GB of RAM; the same person was even able to get the massive Kimi K3 model to run on a single machine…with decoding performance up to 3 tokens/second.

The new live-action Street Fighter movie continues to confound me as its recreations of some characters look hideously stupid and others look delightfully stupid. Still, the movie looks campy in a potentially “so bad it’s good” way, so whatever the case, I will be seated. The latest trailer leans hard into the absurdity by showing off just about everyone in their costumes, and though some characters like Blanka and Guile look kind of off, I guess I have to give it to the movie for just going for it.

As we saw in previous trailers, lead frenemies Ryu and Ken are going through it in this movie, and we get a little bit of insight into why they’re not on the best terms and Chun-Li has to orchestrate a meeting between them at an upcoming tournament (jealousy is at least part of it). Once there, they’ll both encounter plenty of Street Fighter mainstays, such as Dhalsim, Balrog, E. Honda, Guile, Cammy, Zangief, and many, many more characters from Capcom’s fighting games.

It’s still not really clear just how much time the full ensemble cast will get, but either way, Ken and Ryu’s rivalry seems to be the centerpiece holding it all together. M. Bison is also up to something nefarious, though, so we’ll likely see most of the crew band together to stop whatever he’s doing.

articles.title: Apple Announces New M6 and M5 Pro Mac minis, Along with M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studios
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.

The headline feature of the M6 chip is that it’s Apple’s first 2-nanometer chip. The chip also includes “a larger 12-core CPU complex with the world’s fastest CPU core, a larger 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and up to 170GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.”

Looking more closely at the M6, Apple says it consists of two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores and is 1.2x faster in multithreaded performance than an M5 and up to 2.4x faster than an M1. Apple says the GPU delivers nearly 30% more peak GPU compute for AI than the M5. The M6’s 10% faster memory bandwidth will help with AI tasks, too, but its 32GB memory ceiling will limit which models can run locally.

The M6 mini’s GPU sounds impressive, too, with two more cores, Neural Accelerators for each core, which is a first for the mini. According to Apple, that leads to an up to four-fold increase in AI performance and a 2x graphics bump compared to the M4 mini. The Neural Engine has also been improved.

Apple also introduced an M5 Pro mini. It’s understandable if you find it confusing that the base model Mac mini has a more recent generation chipset than the more expensive model. What matters more than the chip generation is the “Pro” in M5 Pro, which makes it more capable than the M6, which has been designed for entry-level models.

The same sort of asymmetry occurred with the 2025 Mac Studio, which included an M4 Max model alongside the M3 Ultra. A big part of that difference is the M5 Pro mini’s support for 64GB of memory (double the M6 version’s top memory spec) and its 307GB/s of memory bandwidth compared to the M6 model’s 170GB/s memory bandwidth.

As for the M5 Ultra, which debuts in the Mac Studio, it sounds like a beast. According to Apple, the chip uses a next-generation version of its UltraFusion technology, resulting in a quad-die architecture for the first time in an Apple silicon chip. In addition, the M5 Ultra features an “up-to-36-core CPU and up-to-80-core GPU with a massive 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, 50 percent more than M3 Ultra.”

Here’s what Sri Santhanam, Apple’s vice president of Silicon Engineering Group, had to say about the new chips:

Today, we’re debuting the next giant leap in performance and AI compute for Apple silicon with the incredibly advanced M6 and the most powerful M-series chip yet, M5 Ultra. Built using the cutting-edge 2 nm process, M6 combines a new CPU complex, two additional CPU and GPU cores, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and more unified memory bandwidth to power through workloads with amazing energy efficiency.

And for the ultimate desktop performance and the ability to run massive AI models, M5 Ultra features a massive GPU, now with Neural Accelerators, and more unified memory bandwidth, pushing the boundaries of what a desktop can do.

Apple is fusing two dual-die M5 Max chips to create a single quad-die architecture. Apple says the M5 Ultra is “up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than M3 Ultra”, the fastest Mac previously for sale. The M5 Ultra also supports up to an 80-core GPU with up to 4.5x the peak GPU compute for AI tasks compared to the M3 Ultra and features an upgraded Media Engine, according to Apple.

For those who don’t need the bleeding-edge performance of the M5 Ultra, Apple also introduced what sounds like a very capable M5 Max Mac Studio. The M5 Max version of the computer “features an 18-core CPU, an up-to-40-core GPU with Neural Accelerators built into each core, and up to 128GB of unified memory, accelerating complex pro and AI workloads.”

Macs featuring the new chips won’t be available immediately. You can preorder both online today for delivery on September 22 with the caveat that the M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 512GB of memory won’t be available until later in October.

Prices have risen too. The Mac mini models are both $100 more than the models they replace, while the M5 Ultra Mac Studio’s base configuration has risen $200. However, the M5 Max Mac Studio’s starting price hasn’t changed.

The Mac mini has been a lot of things to a lot of people over the years. From a compact, minimalist desktop system to a headless server, the mini is Apple’s jack-of-all-trades. More recently, demand for the tiny computer has surged as people put them to work for a variety of AI tasks, including running LLMs locally and serving as standalone Hermes and OpenClaw machines.

With memory and storage constraints, it’s no surprise that the base prices of the mini have risen. Despite those challenges, I hope Apple is able to produce enough to meet demand. I’ve loved having an M4 Pro model working away day and night in the background. It’s fast, relatively cool, energy efficient, and easy to run remotely.

If the claims of Apple’s press release hold up under real-world use, I expect the new models will be the same, but faster and more capable, which is especially important for tasks like running models locally.

I’m also looking forward to seeing how the new Mac Studios perform in real world tests. I’ve used an M1 Max Mac Studio for a few years now and it’s been every bit the workhorse computer I need for my day-to-day work. However, it’s beginning to show its age when it comes to AI tasks, coding, and other tasks. It may finally be time for me to upgrade.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation. Ugly AI graphics and a 50% performance hit, what's not to love?

Word around Nvidia’s already-derided upscaling tech DLSS 5 keeps getting worse. On top of the graphics card manufacturer’s new Deep Learning Super Sampling (DLSS) software churning out ugly AI-generated images, the technology can also cut users’ frame rates in half. Yikes.

PC Gamer’s Andy Edser reported the news after a demo of the technology left him skeptical. While Edser admitted that DLSS 5 looks a bit less hideous when developers get a chance to tweak it, Nvidia told him the technology will reduce frame rates by 50–60% regardless of the game. Since DLSS traditionally improves a game’s frame rate, not the other way around, this news won't fix the software's terrible reputation.

Why does everyone hate DLSS 5?

As for why DLSS 5 has been so controversial, it is a real-time neural rendering model, so it comes with the same ethical and ecological concerns as generative AI. Also, the first DLSS 5 demo looked very bad. Like other forms of generative AI, this software can bulldoze artistic intent. It can make character models look unnatural, transforming them into either conventionally attractive supermodels or specters from the eighth circle of hell.

Although DLSS 5 hasn’t been officially released, a few days ago, players were able to scrape files from an early access build of NBA 2K27 to get it working with other games. While some results weren’t quite as bad as when Nvidia revealed the yassifying tech alongside Resident Evil Requiem, it looks even worse in other cases. Users posted horrifying images of what DLSS 5 looks like in games with an anime aesthetic.

While this tech was never meant to run on many of these games, the situation certainly hasn’t improved Nvidia’s nosediving reputation among many players. Nvidia has profited immensely from the onset of generative AI, and many existing customers have complained that the company has seemingly shifted focus away from traditional gaming as a result.

The company’s most recent graphics cards were criticized as underwhelming, and most players will likely ignore the latest version of DLSS 5 because of the massive performance hit it causes. The controversial software will be released alongside NBA 2K27 on Sept. 3.

While it would be nice to believe this negative feedback will change Nvidia’s trajectory, the company is making so much money off the generative AI craze that this seems a bit unlikely. Until the bubble hopefully pops, PC gamers can likely expect high hardware prices and more dissapointing efforts from Nvidia.

articles.title: How to tap into network debugging
articles.subtitle: I know there’s no connection between my local area network and our house’s plumbing system, but when the faucet started running uncontrollably literally seconds after I fixed a network outage, I had to wonder: did we have a poltergeist?…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
I know there’s no connection between my local area network and our house’s plumbing system, but when the faucet started running uncontrollably literally seconds after I fixed a network outage, I had to wonder: did we have a poltergeist? The jury is still out. But I can tell you that my hour of fruitless examination of router settings is to your benefit: you won’t have to do this when it happens to you.

The weakest TP-Link

As a guy known for Wi-Fi since the early 2000s, you might think my house is ablaze with wireless signals. 1 Yes, it is: we have six Wi-Fi access points and gateways in a relatively small house by modern standards (about 1,200 sq. ft. on the main floor and 800 in the finished basement).

But we also have Ethernet strung through the house to connect most of them, with powerline networking adapters where that doesn’t work due to the ancient and mysterious innards of the walls. The innards’ outsides are covered with heavy, old plaster, which absorbs some of the power of the Wi-Fi signals—hence the large number of emitters.

Normally, this works fine. We have four TP-Link routers, some purchased a while back, and a Netgear Nighthawk as our primary base station, which distributes network addresses and is connected to the fiber-optic ISP router. 2 When something goes wrong, it’s usually an issue with a router crashing, even though its various green lights remain in a happy state.

This time, something was more deeply wrong. The TP-Link routers showed orange Internet connection lights, which in this case meant they were connected via LAN to the Netgear, but they couldn’t reach the Internet. Perversely, I seemed to be able to connect from my iPhone and my office Mac, which has both Ethernet and Wi-Fi connections active. 3

TP-Link has one of the most irritating admin approaches for its routers of nearly any networked product I’ve ever used. You can connect directly, but it’s difficult to store the device’s password because it uses a potentially changing local IP address on your LAN.

There’s also a centralized system where you can use an app called Tether or a TP-Link website to log in remotely to a router, even when you’re on the same LAN, rather than finding its local address. Tether also scans the local network, letting you connect even when Internet access is disrupted.

Without the routers “seeing” the Internet, I couldn’t use the website, and Tether worked erratically. I eventually was able to figure out the IP addresses of two of the four routers, connect via a web browser, and find a working password for one of them. (To reset the password, you have to factory reset the router. That’s for a future day.)

But I remained baffled. My ISP gateway was up. My Mac could reach the Internet. The Netgear router seemed to be routing my Mac’s traffic to the Internet. Some of the devices on our network were also connected to the rest of the world. Had my TP-Link routers been compromised? Was something more sophisticated going on? Nope.

It’s coming from inside your smart house

Some of you may be yelling at me from the safe distance of your phone or computer. “Glenn, Glenn, why didn’t you check DNS?” The circulatory system of the Internet may be the IP-addressed traffic that passes over the series of tubes that make up the network. But DNS is the helpful labeling system, like an editorial cartoon that uses captions like “taxes” and “fat cats” to mark characters in an illustration. DNS turns human-readable domain names into the underlying numbers required for connections.

Surely DNS was working? My iPhone, Mac, and other devices were resolving addresses, or turning them from names into numbers. Then I found a clue in Network Time Protocol (NTP), a somewhat obscure bit of plumbing that also makes things tick. When I went to Advanced: Administration: NTP Settings on the Netgear, the last time it had been able to grab the current time and date was hours earlier. That seemed problematic.

Digging more deeply, literally, I found that the dig Unix command couldn’t pull up IP addresses from the Netgear router. On a LAN in which you’re using DHCP to handle local address assignment, your router may require that you enter Internet IP addresses for one or two DNS servers, or it might retrieve them automatically from your ISP.

When a device on your network requests an address, the DHCP server assigns an address and tells the device to use the router address for DNS resolution. The router relays your requests to the real DNS server.

I tried dig @10.0.0.1 apple.com (use the router to return the IP address for apple.com) via Terminal on my Mac, and it timed out. I then tried the same lookup using my ISP’s DNS servers. Same timeout. The Mac had no problem with domain lookups, however, nor did my iPhone.

Now comes the time to insert a head-slapping emoji. Some time ago, and I can’t recall how long ago, I set my Netgear router to use my ISP’s primary and secondary DNS addresses. I know many people have switched to Google, Quad9, Cloudflare, or other free, public DNS servers to improve lookup speeds, which, at one point, would have helped speed up network operations tremendously because ISPs invested so little in their DNS operations.

However, using public DNS can cause issues in particular cases. For one, it can confuse content delivery networks (CDNs), which try to guess the closest server to you topologically based on your DNS lookup request to their servers. When that works, you’re getting the shortest path and likely faster throughput.

articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Clans of the Forest is due out in just over a month

Trailmark Games has announced that fans will be able to get their hands (paws?) on Warrior Cats: Clans of the Forest in less than two months. The turn-based RPG, based on the long-running young adult series of novels, will be released on Oct. 23.

The developer made the announcement in a new trailer posted to its official YouTube channel. Trailmark Games and the Coolabi Group initially revealed Clans of the Forest this August as the first-ever video game set in the Warrior Cats universe. With less than three months from announcement to release, the wait for the game shouldn't be that grueling for fans.

What is Warrior Cats: Clans of the Forest?

Warrior Cats: Clans of the Forest will be a turn-based RPG that tells an original story with new and familiar faces. Players will be able to customize their own cat and choose between four clans with unique campaigns. In this way, the game evokes the sprawling, multi‑pronged narrative of Fire Emblem: Three Houses. In addition to turn-based combat, Clans of the Forest will have hunting and crafting mechanics.

Beyond the story, players can enjoy the boss-rush Defender mode and the asynchronous multiplayer Skirmish mode.

The Warrior Cats series was initially created by Victoria Holmes for publisher HarperCollins. The first book, Into the Wild, was released in 2003. Since then, it has grown to include over fifty mainline books (and plenty more spin-offs) written by a collective of writers under the pen name Erin Hunter. In addition to the upcoming game, an animated series is currently in the works from Coolabi Group and Tencent Video.

This June, Disney announced it had picked up the show for distribution. The series is slated for release in 2028.

Warrior Cats: Clans of the Forest will be released on Oct. 23 for Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X.

articles.title: Apple ninja edits Mac Studio specs to remove PCIe Gen 6 storage reference
articles.subtitle: Macworld During Apple surprise Mac announcements last week, the company declared in its press release that the Mac Studio features “a next-generation SSD architecture built on PCIe Gen 6.” However, that mention has since been removed from the Mac Studio...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
During Apple surprise Mac announcements last week, the company declared in its press release that the Mac Studio features “a next-generation SSD architecture built on PCIe Gen 6.” However, that mention has since been removed from the Mac Studio press release and site, as spotted by MacGeneration.

The PCIe Gen 6 statement has been removed from the Apple U.K., Apple Germany, and Apple Japan press releases, though strangely, the PCIe Gen 6 reference still exists in the Apple France press release. The releases still list August 25, 2026, as the day of publication and have no record of an update, but we, along with many other outlets, quoted the PCIe Gen 6 in our original stories and haven’t been contacted by Apple about a correction.

The press release now reads, “Storage performance is up to twice as fast, with a next-generation SSD architecture, delivering industry-leading read and write speeds for rapid project loading, file transfers, and loading huge LLMs.” The twice as fast comparision is to the M3 Ultra Mac Studio.

The Internet Archive has a copy of the U.S. Mac Studio press release, recorded on August 25 at 13:03:29, and it contains the PCIe Gen 6 reference. Other copies recorded by the Internet Archive on August 25 still have the reference, but the first record of the press release on August 26 at 02:03:13 shows that the release was revised to remove references to PCIe Gen 6.

PCIe Gen 6 is the next generation of the PCIe interconnect standard, offering performance upgrades over the PCIe Gen 5 standard. Apple did not specify that the M5 Ultra Mac Studio implements PCIe Gen 5, but the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips are equipped with it. So it’s likely that the M5 Ultra has it too, and Apple made an error in its press release.

Apple was contacted for clarification and had yet to respond at the time of this posting.

Well, this seems interesting. ChatGPT’s latest update adds a new Mac integration: the ability to work with conversations from Apple’s Messages app. The feature works with iMessage, SMS, and RCS.

ChatGPT for Mac now includes an Apple Messages plugin

The new Apple Messages plugin lets ChatGPT read and search chats on a Mac, and prepare and send messages.

OpenAI says it is available across all plans in the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS, with support in both ChatGPT Work and Codex.

That access raises privacy and control questions, so OpenAI stresses that sending remains gated by user approval under the default settings.

Users should take care before granting persistent approval. OpenAI’s plugin guide details the risks and how to revoke access.

It also lists a known issue involving tasks that disable approval prompts: “If your task is set to Full access or otherwise disables approval prompts, Apple Messages may be unable to show the confirmation needed to send. Switch to Ask for approval or Approve for me and try again.”

How OpenAI’s Messages plugin works on the Mac

OpenAI explains that the optional Messages plugin runs locally on the Mac. Like other ChatGPT/Codex features including Computer Use, it relies on macOS system technologies like AppleScript and Accessibility.

The optional Messages plugin is not like the sketchy server-related hacks that try to bring iMessage functionality to Android. It’s simply using files on your Mac with your permission when prompted.

And unlike Siri AI, it doesn’t rely on an index of content from Messages. ChatGPT for Mac only uses the data when directed and with permission.

As you can see below, once enabled by the user, ChatGPT is super clear in what it does with messages, especially sending on your behalf when asked.

For these reasons, it shouldn’t be a privacy concern for Apple. The data exists as files on your Mac, and you need to give ChatGPT permission to work with the files. OpenAI also isn’t the only AI company to develop similar tools. It’s just a benefit of the Mac being a more capable operating system than mobile platforms.

articles.title: Siri demos in keynote were a little slow, but that’s good-ish news
articles.subtitle: A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: Warlock Won’t Have One of Baldur’s Gate 3’s Most Beloved D&D Mechanics
articles.subtitle: Kaatri ain't doing much smoochin' Baldur's Gate 3 is the best Dungeons & Dragons video game of all time, and anyone trying to argue otherwise has a tall order on their hands.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Kaatri ain't doing much smoochin'

Baldur's Gate 3 is the best Dungeons & Dragons video game of all time, and anyone trying to argue otherwise has a tall order on their hands. It embodies everything D&D stands for: freedom and player choice, a branching narrative, and skill checks represented by so, so many dice rolls.

One aspect of Larian Studios' masterpiece that players love most is its romance options. However, despite the fact Warlock is another AAA D&D game in the works, it won't be following suit. Sorry, horny folks on the internet: that means you can't watch Kaatri and Tasha get it on.

In an interview at Gamescom 2026, Dominic Guay, studio head at Invoke Studios, told Polygon that "romancing is out of the question for now in her life," because "she has a quest that she's really dead set on." While it's still an open-world game, Warlock is much narrower in terms of player choice than Baldur's Gate 3, so there's just one core story to experience.

"She will meet other characters, not just monsters," Guay continued. "She'll kind of have a found family." He highlighted Skev, an imp who accompanies Kaatri throughout her journey, as an example: "There's going to be a growing relationship there, but she's also going to meet other characters, but there's no actual romancing options within those relationships."

Image: Invoke Studios/Wizards of the Coast

When I asked about how much development we can expect to see with Kaatri as a character, Guay explained that while "she's very set on her quests," the player will "discover more and more layers of her personality. One of the benefits of having a written story is that we can go all into that. We can realize it with the full level of detail in our cinematics and make sure that we nail these critical story beats to tell the story we want to tell."

So there we have it, folks. Dungeons & Dragons sounds like it's more of a setting and idea for Warlock, but it won't dictate everything the game will offer, thanks to the devs wanting to provide a more crafted experience. Another consequence of this is that the game won't be hundreds of hours long, either.
